title: Σπάλαξ ⟨καὶ μήτηρ⟩
part: The Mole and his Mother (Chambry 326 · Perry 214)
source: Émile Chambry, Ésope: Fables, texte établi et traduit (Les Belles Lettres, Paris, 1927), fable 326 (= Perry 214). Text as printed, including Chambry's editorial punctuation (« », ⟨ ⟩ for editorial supplements, [ ] for words Chambry deletes as interpolated). Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; accents omitted).

sentences.t: Σπάλαξ (ἐστὶ δὲ τοῦτο τὸ ζῷον τυφλόν) λέγει πρὸς τὴν ἑαυτοῦ μητέρα ὅτι βλέπει.
sentences.tr: Spalax (esti de touto to zōion typhlon) legei pros tēn heautou mētera hoti blepei.
sentences.l: A mole (and this animal is blind) says to his own mother that he sees.
sentences.n: The parenthesis stands in the text as Chambry prints it — it is none of his editorial brackets (⟨ ⟩ for supplements, [ ] for deletions) — and tells the reader plainly that the animal cannot see. λέγει is a narrative present; βλέπει after ὅτι keeps the tense of the mole's own words — he said 'I see'.

sentences.t: Κἀκείνη πειράζουσα αὐτὸν χόνδρον λιβανωτοῦ δοῦσα ἐπηρώτα τί ποτε εἴη.
sentences.tr: Kakeinē peirazousa auton chondron libanōtou dousa epērōta ti pote eiē.
sentences.l: And she, testing him, having given him a grain of frankincense, kept asking what ever it might be.
sentences.i: And she, to put him to the test, gave him a grain of frankincense and asked what on earth it was.
sentences.n: Κἀκείνη is καὶ ἐκείνη run together by crasis. χόνδρος is a lump or grain of the resin — the point is that frankincense declares itself to the nose long before the eye. εἴη is optative in an indirect question after the past tense ἐπηρώτα, the regular shift; ποτε attached to an interrogative is 'ever, on earth'.

sentences.t: Τοῦ δὲ εἰπόντος ψηφῖδα, ἔφη· « Ὦ τέκνον, οὐ μόνον τοῦ βλέπειν ἐστέρησαι, ἀλλὰ καὶ τὰς ὀσφρήσεις ἀποβέβλησαι. »
sentences.tr: Tou de eipontos psēphida, ephē· « Ō teknon, ou monon tou blepein esterēsai, alla kai tas osphrēseis apobeblēsai. »
sentences.l: And he having said 'a pebble', she said: « O child, not only have you been deprived of seeing, but you have thrown away your sense of smell as well. »
sentences.i: And when he said it was a pebble, she said: « My child, you have not only been robbed of your sight — you have thrown away your sense of smell into the bargain. »
sentences.n: A genitive absolute (τοῦ … εἰπόντος), with the accusative ψηφῖδα left standing as the whole of his answer. στερέομαι takes a genitive of what one is deprived of, here the articular infinitive τοῦ βλέπειν, 'of seeing'. ἀποβέβλησαι is a perfect middle of ἀποβάλλω, and the accusative τὰς ὀσφρήσεις after it shows the middle rather than the passive: he has cast the thing away himself. The Greek plural, the faculties of smell taken together, is an English singular.

sentences.t: Οὕτως ἔνιοι τῶν ἀλαζόνων, [μέχρις οὗ] τὰ ἀδύνατα κατεπαγγέλλονται, καὶ ἐν τοῖς ἐλαχίστοις ἐξελέγχονται.
sentences.tr: Houtōs enioi tōn alazonōn, [mechris hou] ta adynata katepangellontai, kai en tois elachistois exelenchontai.
sentences.l: Thus some among the braggarts, [so long as] they profess impossible things, are shown up even in the very smallest matters.
sentences.i: Thus some braggarts profess the impossible and are shown up in the very smallest things.
sentences.n: Chambry brackets [μέχρις οὗ] as a later intrusion; with it gone the sentence runs straight on, 'some braggarts profess the impossible and are shown up…'. κατεπαγγέλλομαι is to undertake for a thing in large terms, the κατα- giving it the note of boasting. ἐξελέγχω is to convict, to catch a man out.
